name: mlkem-native (pq-code-package)
baseline: mlkem-native's own portable C backend (CI 'no-opt' rows, native backends disabled); that C code is a C90 fork of the pq-crystals/kyber ref implementation and is what liboqs ships as its portable C ML-KEM since 0.13.0
workload: Cycle counts per ML-KEM-512/768/1024 keypair, encaps and decaps from the project's CI benchmark job (./scripts/tests bench, PMU/PERF cycle counters), native AArch64 (SLOTHY-optimised Neon, HOL-Light-verified) and x86-64 AVX2 assembly backends against the portable C backend of the same tree, on AWS EC2 Graviton2-5, Intel Xeon 3rd/4th gen and AMD EPYC 3rd/4th gen instances.
claimed_speedup: (derived from page data) ML-KEM-768 cycles, C backend divided by native backend, repo commit aad9b74 (2026-10-12 CI run): Intel Xeon 4th gen c7i keypair 46550 -> 19302 (2.41x), encaps 55352 -> 20638 (2.68x), decaps 67682 -> 26122 (2.59x); AMD EPYC 4th gen c7a 59740 -> 21586 (2.77x), 67717 -> 22806 (2.97x), 84577 -> 29706 (2.85x); Graviton2 keypair 96838 -> 47604 (2.03x), encaps 109796 -> 53830 (2.04x), decaps 134838 -> 68518 (1.97x); Graviton4 1.97x / 1.98x / 1.90x. Range over the 8 EC2 targets for ML-KEM-768: 1.9x to 3.0x.
compiler_and_flags: Common flags from config.mk: -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -std=c99 -pedantic; per-target flags from .github/workflows/bench.yml: all EC2 rows add -flto and -DMLK_FORCE_AARCH64 or -DMLK_FORCE_X86_64; arch flags e.g. c7i: -mavx2 -mbmi2 -mpopcnt -march=sapphirerapids, c7a: -march=znver4, c6i: -march=icelake-server, c6a: -march=znver3, Graviton2: -mcpu=cortex-a76 -march=armv8.2-a, Graviton3: -march=armv8.4-a+sha3, Graviton4/5: -march=armv9-a+sha3. Compiler version not stated in the opened files (default nix dev shell gcc; the version is only printed in the CI step summary).
hardware: AWS EC2: c7i.metal-24xl (Intel Xeon 4th gen), c6i.large (Intel Xeon 3rd gen), c7a.medium (AMD EPYC 4th gen), c6a.large (AMD EPYC 3rd gen), t4g.small (Graviton2), c7g.medium (Graviton3), c8g.medium (Graviton4), c9g.medium (Graviton5); self-hosted Raspberry Pi 4/5, Snapdragon 888 A55, SpacemiT K1, Apple M1, POWER10 and Cortex-M55 rows also exist in data.js.
stars_or_usage: 247 stars; default ML-KEM in liboqs since 0.13.0, in AWS-LC since v1.50.0 (and so rustls via AWS-LC), per the README
tradeoffs: AArch64 and x86-64 assembly is formally proved functionally correct, memory-safe and constant-time with HOL-Light, C code proved memory- and type-safe with CBMC; assembly exists only for AArch64 (Neon), x86-64 (AVX2), plus RISC-V RVV and POWER VSX backends; build is import-the-sources, the repo's Makefile is for development only; ML-KEM only (no ML-DSA).
caveats: The only measured comparison found is native backend against the project's own C backend, not against the unmodified pq-crystals/kyber ref or liboqs portable C directly; the C backend is itself an optimised fork of ref, so the gap to the plain reference code is likely larger. The data.js file holds a rolling history, the numbers above are the latest points (commit aad9b74); they move with every main-branch commit. The rendered page https://pq-code-package.github.io/mlkem-native/dev/bench/ is egress-blocked here, the raw gh-pages data.js file was read instead. EC2 rows are VM timings from CI (c7i is bare metal, others are small shared instance types). Compiler and version for the EC2 jobs are not visible in the opened files. No independent third-party run found. A SLOTHY paper (eprint 2022/1303, blocked) has earlier NTT-level results on Cortex-A55/A72 that were not read.

name: aes-armcortexm (Schwabe and Stoffelen, Cortex-M3/M4 AES assembly)
baseline: RIOT OS default C AES implementation (third-party forum report); the SAC 2016 paper compares against unnamed prior Cortex-M AES implementations; the repo README names no baseline
workload: AES-128 single-block encryption and decryption latency in microseconds on an STM32L151 (Cortex-M3) after integration into RIOT OS, per a forum post seen only as a search snippet; the repo README itself gives cycle counts for the assembly only (AES-128 single block 637.5 cycles on Cortex-M3 STM32L100C, 634.7 on Cortex-M4 STM32F407; AES-128 CTR 531.8 / 527.9 cycles per block; averaged over 4096 bytes and 10000 runs).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (page not opened, egress blocked): RIOT forum post reports assembler version 45 us per encode and 87 us per decode against 74 us and 131 us for RIOT's default implementation on an STM32L151 (derived from snippet: about 1.6x encrypt, 1.5x decrypt). Paper abstract (snippet only): 'about twice as fast as existing implementations'. Repo README: absolute cycles only (see workload), no baseline.
hardware: STM32L151 (Cortex-M3) for the forum numbers; STM32L100C (Cortex-M3) and STM32F407 (Cortex-M4) development boards for the README table
stars_or_usage: 97 stars; integrated into RIOT OS per a forum post (snippet); jnk0le/cortexm-AES says its CM3_1T implementation is originally based on this code
tradeoffs: Fully unrolled code (about 2 KB code for AES-128 block, 1 KB T-table data; ROM can be reduced at small cost); the fast table-based variants are not advertised as constant time (the separate bitsliced constant-time AES-128-CTR, about 1617 cycles per block, and a first-order masked variant for M4 are); the masked variant needs a hardware RNG and is STM32F407 specific; Cortex-M3/M4 only, GNU as Thumb-2 syntax, build uses libopencm3 submodule.
caveats: The repo README has absolute cycle numbers but compares against nothing, and does not mention reference C AES or mbedTLS. The two comparison datapoints (RIOT forum timings, 'about twice as fast' in the SAC 2016 paper 'All the AES You Need on Cortex-M3 and M4') come from search-result snippets only: eprint.iacr.org, ko.stoffelen.nl and forum.riot-os.org all fail to resolve here (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so tier is capped at C and the paper's comparison table was not read; a verifier with paper access should check whether it supports B. The forum post gives no compiler flags or clock speed in the snippet. Repo is old (last commit 2020-07-12, README benchmark refresh); CC0 dedication has no patent grant. Later Cortex-M AES work exists (jnk0le/cortexm-AES, aadomn/aes fixslicing) and was not compared here.

name: FreeBSD libmd md5block.S (amd64 baseline, BMI1 and AVX-512 MD5 kernels)
baseline: libmd's C MD5 block function: the 'orig' build (previous md5c.c) and the new 'generic' C build measured in the same review
workload: MD5 hashing throughput in MB/s over a large input (run times of roughly 10-14 s per variant), comparing libmd variants orig, generic, baseline, bmi1 and avx512 in the D45670 review; method and exact command not visible in the snippet.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (page not opened): Ryzen 7 PRO 7840U (Zen 4): orig 774.6 MB/s, generic 758.5, baseline asm 945.5, bmi1 asm 1062.4, avx512 asm 936.0 (derived from snippet: bmi1 1.40x over generic, 1.37x over orig). Core i7-1165G7 (Tiger Lake): orig about 606 MB/s, generic 587.8, baseline asm 765.3, bmi1 854.0, avx512 965.1 (derived from snippet: avx512 1.64x over generic).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 7840U (Zen 4) and 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 (Tiger Lake), per search snippet
stars_or_usage: 9.4k stars on the freebsd-src publish-only mirror; kernels imported by commit d92e987 'lib/libmd: import md5 amd64 kernels' (2025-10-24), file lib/libmd/amd64/md5block.S by Robert Clausecker (BSD-2-Clause)
tradeoffs: Three kernels selected at load time by an ifunc resolver (lib/libmd/amd64/md5dispatch.c): AVX-512 (vpternlogd, XMM-only) when AVX512F and AVX512VL are present and the vendor is not AMD, else BMI1 (ANDN shortens dependency chains), else the baseline scalar kernel. The review snippet says the kernel build reuses the new code except the AVX-512 path (FPU state cost). Single-stream MD5 (no multi-buffer); MD5 itself is cryptographically broken, only for compatibility and checksums. amd64 only.
caveats: The task lead said the commit message quotes the numbers; it does not. The commit page https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/commit/d92e987421001c365216b039f8c3303939c195f7 (opened) holds only the title and 'Differential Revision: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D45670'. reviews.freebsd.org, reviews-dev.freebsd.org and cgit.freebsd.org fail to resolve here (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so every number above comes from WebSearch result snippets of the D45670 review and is snippet only (tier capped at C); the benchmark_url was not opened. Compiler, flags, input size and command are unknown, and OpenSSL MD5 is not a compared baseline. The snippet calls the comparison point 'generic', the C identification is inferred. The 'orig' Tiger Lake figure (about 606 MB/s) is rounded in the snippet. Author-run on two laptop CPUs, one run each as far as visible. A related review (D52909) snippet says the author noticed a performance regression on Zen 4 when moving md5 code, so Zen 4 results may have been revisited after these numbers. Dispatch comment in md5dispatch.c states the AVX-512 kernel performs poorly on AMD, which is why it is skipped there.

name: leancrypto ML-KEM RISC-V assembly and RVV (PQRV-derived)
baseline: leancrypto's own pure-C ML-KEM (Kyber) implementation, built from the same tree without the riscv64 ASM operations
workload: Wall-clock time of the ml-kem/tests/kyber_kem_tester_common performance run ('c' argument, large round count of keygen, encaps and decaps; parameter set not stated in the commit message), C against the RISC-V assembly build.
claimed_speedup: Commit 3caa605 'ML-KEM: add RISCV64 assembler implementation' (2024-11-24): 'The performance almost doubles: ml-kem/tests/kyber_kem_tester_common c - C: 123s - ASM: 65s' (derived from page data: 1.89x).
stars_or_usage: 97 stars; ACVP-tested on a SpacemiT X60 K1 RISC-V board among others
tradeoffs: The RISC-V ML-KEM code (ml-kem/src/riscv64: ntt_dualissue_plant_rv64im.S plus RVV vlen128 and vlen256 NTT and polynomial code, runtime-selected between ASM, RVV-128 and RVV-256) is derived from Ji-Peng/PQRV (MIT, Zhang Jipeng, TCHES 2025); leancrypto's own C is a separate Kyber implementation. RVV paths need the V extension; PR #20 (2025-03-07) added a CPU feature check before the RVV selector. Library is aimed at bare metal, Linux kernel and user space, with other ML-KEM backends for ARMv7, ARMv8 and AVX2.
caveats: Lead in the task named 'Issue #2' of leancrypto; that issue is an unrelated Linux-kernel Kbuild error (opened 2023-06-27). The ~60% figure is in issue #2 of Ji-Peng/PQRV, 'Spacemit X60: RVV implementation causes SIGBUS' (https://github.com/Ji-Peng/PQRV/issues/2, opened 2024-11-24, closed 2024-11-26; opened this session): a maintainer comment dated 2025-02-02 says 'Performance boost by almost 60% on Spacemit X60: for ML-KEM 1024 when performing 50,000 rounds of keygen/enc/dec, with RISCV asm it takes about 49.3s vs 31s with RVV 256' (derived 1.59x). That compares RVV-256 against the RISC-V assembly path, not against C, and was run on a SpacemiT X60 (VLEN=256) with no compiler or flags stated. The commit-message figure names no board, compiler, flags or parameter set and the test harness may have changed since; it is a first-party single-run anecdote. No bench tables exist in the repo README (only a performance goal statement). Licence is inferred from LICENSE.bsd and LICENSE.gplv2 (dual BSD-3-Clause/GPL-2.0 is assumed, the LICENSE file says 'See LICENSE.* for the applicable license'); the repo also carries per-file MIT, Apache-2.0, CC0 and GPL-3 (duplicated compiler code) notices from upstream sources, all OSI or public domain.

name: lazypoline (hybrid SUD plus binary-rewriting syscall interposer)
baseline: zpoline (binary rewriting) and pure Syscall User Dispatch (SUD) interposition; the paper also discusses ptrace and seccomp-based interposition but the artifact scripts opened here only run baseline, zpoline, lazypoline and SUD variants
workload: DSN 2024 artifact (github.com/lazypoline/benchmarks): bench/bench_micro.sh runs a syscall microbenchmark pinned to one core, 10 repetitions, for plain syscall baseline, zpoline, lazypoline with SUD interposition, SUD enabled without interposition, lazypoline after rewriting, SUD disabled and with extended-state (vector) preservation; bench_nginx.sh and bench_lighttpd.sh drive nginx and lighttpd with 12 workers and wrk.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on any opened page. README and artifact give no results; they are in Table II and Figures 4 and 5 of the DSN 2024 paper 'System Call Interposition Without Compromise' (egress-blocked). Qualitative claim in README: 'fast, exhaustive, and expressive'; paper abstract (search snippet) claims the efficiency of pure rewriting for syscall-intensive workloads.
hardware: 48-core Intel Xeon Gold 5318S at 2.10 GHz, 1.0 TiB RAM, hyperthreading disabled, Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS, Linux 5.15.0-83 (benchmarks README)
stars_or_usage: 32 stars; peer-reviewed at IEEE/IFIP DSN 2024 (pp. 183-194); superseded by the same group's Secpoline (USENIX Security 2026)
tradeoffs: Needs Linux 5.11+ (SUD) and permission to mmap the zero page (vm.mmap_min_addr=0) like zpoline; exhaustive interposition of dynamically generated code that zpoline misses (the artifact's exhaustiveness test shows zpoline missing getpid from tcc-generated code); not isolated from a malicious application (that is what Secpoline adds); tested on Ubuntu 20.04 and 22.04 glibc 2.35; per the paper abstract (search snippet) each syscall site is first caught through the slow kernel SUD path and only then rewritten, so first executions cost more than later ones.
caveats: No usable numbers: the DSN paper (adriaanjacobs.github.io, repository.tudelft.nl, zenodo) is egress-blocked and neither README nor the artifact repo prints results, so the tier is D although the work is peer reviewed and the benchmark scripts are public (compiler and flags not described; the artifact repo has no licence file and 0 stars). A third-party table seen only as a search snippet (SysComb, arXiv 2608.26871, getpid x 1e6 on Linux 6.8: native about 166 ns, ptrace 11,931 ns, SUD 2,658 ns, zpoline 198 ns) does not include lazypoline. By design lazypoline is not expected to beat zpoline on raw latency; its claim is near-zpoline cost with exhaustiveness, and a large gain over SUD-only and ptrace. The latest commit (2026-06-15) is a README edit; last code change 2025-04-21 ('redzone fix'). A verifier with paper access should read Table II and could raise this to B or A.

name: Souper (LLVM IR superoptimizer)
baseline: stock LLVM optimisation pipeline output (clang -O2/-O3 without Souper)
workload: Code size of a Clang/LLVM binary compiled with an automatic Souper-based optimisation pass, against the stock LLVM-built binary, per the arXiv 1711.04422 abstract (search snippet only). This is a code-size claim, not an execution-speed claim.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (page not opened): 'A fully automated optimization pass built with Souper yields a Clang binary about 3 MB (4.4%) smaller than the one LLVM produces.' No SPEC or other execution-time speedups found in any reachable source; the README gives no numbers.
stars_or_usage: 2.4k stars, 188 forks; suggested optimisations were hand-implemented in LLVM and MSVC per the paper abstract; repo archived 2025-10-30
tradeoffs: Needs an SMT solver (Z3 via -z3-path) and builds its own LLVM/Clang through build_deps.sh (last bump to LLVM 18 in May 2024); runs as an LLVM opt pass or the sclang/sclang++ drop-in compilers and adds compile time (the README says Redis query caching 'often gives a substantial speedup for large compilations'); targets LLVM IR peephole expressions; archived, so no further LLVM tracking.
caveats: arxiv.org, ar5iv and web mirrors fail to resolve here (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the abstract claim is snippet only and the paper's evaluation (any SPEC CPU speedups or LLVM versions and flags) was not read; the lead's 'speedups on SPEC' could not be confirmed and the abstract snippet mentions no SPEC speedups. The one number is binary size, which does not fit the project's 'faster' qualification; kept as a tooling entry. Repo README and RESULTS file list bug reports and LLVM commits attributed to Souper, with no performance data. The paper is first-party (arXiv, not confirmed peer reviewed). Successor work Minotaur (already on the known list) reports speedups against Souper. Archived 2025-10-30, last commit 2024-08-28 ('StringRef::startswith was deprecated, use starts_with').
